outputs.L1:
“You look sleazy tonight,” Ma said.

“Cheap,” I said. “I’m doin’ cheap. You got any idea how much it costs to do cheap these days? To do gold City of Paris three-inch platform sandals and this I. Magnin snake dress? I’m doin’ cheap.”

“You look like a bird,” she said, “a Halloween bird with red-waxed lips.”

In high school, you could either do cheap or Shakespeare—college prep or a pointy bra, ratting a bubble haircut with a toilet brush. I was not allowed to do high-school cheap; I did blazers and wool skirts from the Junior League thrift shop. In high school, it was: “Don’t walk in the middle of Richie, Leelee, and the baby. You might come between them.”

“You look like a skag wearin’ that black-eyed makeup. People are gunna think you’re cheap.”

While I poured red food dye on my hair to match my filly’s tail for the rodeo, Ma beat her head against the wall, she said, tryin’ to make me nice. I tried real hard, but the loggers, the Navy guys—they always hit on me.

“’Cause you’re an easy mark,” Ma said.

And I played guilty. I played guilty every time.

“But now,” I said, “now I’m doin’ cheap.”
outputs.L2:
Ma told me I looked trashy that night.

“Not trashy—cheap,” I replied. “That’s the effect I’m going for. Do you know what it costs nowadays to look cheap? Gold three-inch platform shoes from City of Paris, plus a snakeskin dress from I. Magnin—that’s my version of cheap.”

She said I resembled some kind of bird: a Halloween creature with glossy, wax-red lips.

Back in high school, the choices seemed to be tawdry or Shakespeare, pointy bras or college-prep clothes, with a puffed-up bubble hairstyle teased using a toilet brush. I wasn’t permitted to choose the tawdry option. Instead, I wore blazers and wool skirts bought at the Junior League thrift store. Those years were full of warnings: don’t walk between Richie, Leelee, and their baby, or you might divide the family; don’t wear dark, bruised-looking eye makeup because it makes you look like a skag and people will decide you’re cheap.

For the rodeo, I poured red food coloring over my hair so it would match my young mare’s tail. Meanwhile, Ma knocked her head against the wall, saying she was struggling to turn me into a respectable girl. I honestly tried. Even so, lumberjacks and Navy men kept making advances toward me.

Ma said it happened because I looked like an easy target. Each time, I accepted the blame and acted ashamed.

“But that was then,” I said. “Now I’m deliberately going cheap.”
outputs.L3:
The narrator deliberately embraces an appearance that might be dismissed as “cheap,” even though achieving it requires expensive clothing, platform sandals, heavy makeup, and carefully painted red lips. Her mother reacts harshly to this style, describing it as sleazy and birdlike and warning that it will cause others to judge her negatively.

This conflict has deep roots in the narrator’s adolescence. In high school, she was forbidden from wearing provocative clothes and instead dressed in conservative secondhand blazers and wool skirts. Her mother was determined to make her look “nice” and respectable, even as the narrator began experimenting with more dramatic forms of self-expression, such as dyeing her hair for a rodeo.

The narrator’s present style is therefore more than a fashion choice. For years, she was blamed for attracting unwanted attention from men and repeatedly accepted responsibility for their behavior. Now, however, she rejects that imposed guilt. By defiantly adopting the very identity she was once denied and taught to fear, she turns her appearance into an act of rebellion, self-definition, and control.
outputs.L4:
The narrator’s conflict with her mother centers on the accusation that she looks “cheap,” but the word carries far more weight than a simple criticism of clothing or appearance. For the mother, respectability seems to depend on controlling how a woman presents herself and how others—especially men—respond to her. Her judgments reflect gendered and class-based expectations: a respectable woman must appear modest, restrained, and socially acceptable, while any display of sexuality or individuality risks being treated as evidence of moral failure. The narrator is therefore taught to regard her body and self-expression as potential sources of shame.

Through flashbacks, the text reveals that these expectations have shaped the narrator for years. Memories of enforced respectability show how she was expected to monitor herself in order to avoid gossip, judgment, or unwanted male attention. Yet this logic unfairly makes her responsible for men’s behavior. Rather than criticizing those who objectify her, the adults around her encourage her to feel guilty for being noticed. Respectability becomes a form of discipline: it promises protection and social approval, but only if she suppresses parts of herself.

The narrator’s defiant dialogue with her mother disrupts this pattern. Instead of quietly accepting the label “cheap,” she challenges the assumptions behind it. Her resistance exposes the way the insult combines judgments about gender, sexuality, and class. To look “cheap” is not merely to dress in a certain way; it is to be placed outside an ideal of respectable femininity associated with self-denial and social conformity. The mother’s criticism may come from fear and from her own experience of social judgment, but it nevertheless reproduces the same system that has made both women vulnerable to shame.

By deciding to “do cheap,” the narrator transforms the insult into a deliberate choice. She no longer allows the word to function as a weapon against her. Instead, she reclaims the stigmatized identity and uses it to assert control over her body and appearance. This choice does not necessarily mean that she accepts society’s negative definition of “cheap.” Rather, she rejects the authority of those who use the label to limit her.

Her final act is therefore both personal and political. She refuses to carry guilt for men’s attention, and she refuses to treat self-expression as a moral failure. In embracing what she has been taught to fear, the narrator breaks with inherited standards of respectability and claims the right to define herself on her own terms.
outputs.L5:
### You, Me, and the Cheap City

You arrive in the city with a small bag, a thin wallet, and a long list of dreams. Nothing here is cheap—not the rent, not the coffee, not even the silence. Still, you learn its secret paths: the corner shop with warm bread, the free concerts in the park, and the buses that carry you past glittering towers for the price of a coin.

The city may be expensive, but a good life doesn’t have to be. You find friendship on crowded sidewalks, beauty in old buildings, and hope beneath the neon lights. With curiosity and courage, even a cheap evening can feel priceless.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a gritty first-person monologue in fragmented, experimental prose about a woman defiantly dressing “cheap” despite her mother’s lifelong attempts to make her respectable.
counterfactuals.output:
I wear the hoops big enough to catch a fist.

Gold-colored. Not gold. Let the distinction glitter.

My mother used to pinch price tags between two fingers like they were dead flies. Polyester. Acrylic. Vinyl. She taught me fabrics the way other mothers taught prayers: wool, silk, linen—natural fibers, natural manners, natural consequences. She believed a woman could be saved by a good hem.

Stand straight.

Cross your ankles.

Don’t chew gum.

Don’t dress like—

She never finished. Didn’t have to. The word was always there, barefoot in the doorway.

Cheap.

So I wear the red dress. The one that shines under streetlights like spilled cough syrup. It rides up when I walk. I let it. I wear boots made of plastic pretending to be snakeskin, and lashes thick as black feathers. My lipstick costs less than bus fare and leaves evidence on everything: cups, cigarettes, collars, the back of my hand.

My mother calls this a waste.

Not the clothes. Me.

She spent her life ironing the girl out of me. Steam. Starch. Pressure. She pressed every wild crease flat. Bought me navy skirts. Pearl studs. A beige coat with buttons like small, obedient moons. Said, You want people to take you seriously.

People.

Meaning men with offices.

Women with soft voices.

Store clerks who watched us differently when she carried the leather handbag.

Meaning anybody who could hurt us and call it policy.

She thought respectability was armor. Didn’t understand armor can become a coffin if you sleep in it long enough.

I learned early: the world will name your price no matter what you’re wearing.

So tonight—mesh. Leopard print. Rhinestones shedding from my purse like loose teeth. A silver chain around my waist, green at the clasp. I smell like drugstore vanilla and rain in hot pavement.

I look magnificent.

I look like every warning she swallowed.

In the mirror, I can hear her clicking her tongue from three neighborhoods away. I can feel her hands come up behind me, trying to tug the neckline higher, trying to hide the soft animal fact of my body. Her hands were always fixing. Fixing meant loving. Loving meant fear.

I know that now.

Still.

I pull the neckline lower.

Not for the men leaning out of car windows. Not for the women who scan me and decide they know my rent, my education, my damage. Not even for her.

For me.

For the girl in the beige coat, sweating through the lining.

For the girl who learned to sit without taking space.

For the girl who mistook disappearance for dignity.

I dress cheap because cheap survives. Cheap cracks, peels, loses stones on the dance floor. Cheap gets rained on. Cheap gets laughed at and comes back louder. Cheap knows exactly what it is and does not ask permission to shine.

My mother wanted me respectable.

Respectable to whom?

Tonight I step into the street with my fake gold blazing, my skirt climbing, my mouth red and reckless.

Let them look.

Let them count the ways I failed to become her good coat hanging untouched in a dark closet.

I was never made to last like that.

I was made to be worn.

Worn out.

Worn loud.

Alive.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a short literary passage centered on the repeated line “I’m doin cheap,” incorporating designer platform sandals, a snakeskin dress, high-school memories, rodeos, loggers, Navy men, and a judgmental mother.
counterfactuals.output:
“I’m doin cheap,” Lila said, buckling her designer platform sandals beneath a snakeskin dress that flashed like river water.

Her mother looked her over with the same pinched expression she’d worn at Lila’s high-school graduation. Back then, Lila had dreamed of rodeos, loggers with cedar in their hair, and Navy men who sent postcards from blue horizons.

“I’m doin cheap,” she repeated, though nothing she wore was cheap and nothing she remembered had been easy.

Outside, the fairground lights shivered awake. Somewhere, a bronco struck the earth like thunder. Her mother sighed.

Lila smiled, taller now in those impossible shoes.

“I’m doin cheap,” she said, and stepped toward the music.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a raw, dialogue-driven prose poem in which a mother tells her daughter she looks sleazy, cheap, and birdlike, while the daughter reclaims that image as an act of rebellion.
counterfactuals.output:
“You look sleazy,” my mother says,  
pinching the air above my skirt  
as if she could hem me without touching me.

“Good,” I say. “Sleaze survives.”

“You look cheap.”

“Then no man gets to call me priceless  
and lock me in a velvet box.”

She circles me with her mouth tightened.  
The kitchen light hums like an interrogation.

“And those feathers—God. You look birdlike.”

I lift my arms. Black fringe trembles  
from wrist to shoulder.

“What kind of bird?” I ask.

“The kind that eats off roads.  
The kind that screams at dawn.  
All bones and sharp eyes.”

“A crow, then.”

“A scavenger.”

“A witness.”

“A pest.”

“A choir.”

She says, “I raised you better.”

I say, “You raised me with windows closed.”

She says, “People will stare.”

I say, “Let them learn where to put their eyes.”

Outside, night spreads its oily wing  
over the roofs. My boots wait by the door,  
scuffed silver at the toes,  
beautiful as small weapons.

My mother whispers, “You look like trouble.”

I kiss her cheek, leaving one dark print.

“No,” I tell her. “I look like escape.”

Then I go out—  
cheap glitter, sleazy halo,  
bird-boned and loud—  
not falling,

not ruined,

but beating the whole black sky  
into flight.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an edgy stream-of-consciousness vignette narrated by a woman remembering how she was pushed toward blazers, Shakespeare, and respectability instead of makeup, provocative clothes, and working-class femininity.
counterfactuals.output:
They put me in a blazer like they were covering a stain.

Navy blue, brass buttons, shoulders squared into little upholstered lies. *You look smart,* Mum said, which meant safe, which meant not like the women smoking outside the salon in leopard print, laughing with their whole throats. Not like Auntie June with her silver hoops and supermarket perfume and cleavage pushed up like a dare. Not like girls who wrote their names in lip liner on the bus shelter. Smart meant Shakespeare tucked under one arm and all the loud parts of me held under the other, sweating.

Lady Macbeth, yes. Mascara, no.

They praised me whenever I disappeared correctly. Hair scraped back. Skirt to the knee. Voice ironed flat. I learned words like *ambition* and *gravitas* and *university*, learned to say them without the accent thickening around the edges. At parents’ evening, teachers smiled as though they’d rescued me from a burning building.

“She has such potential.”

Potential for what? To leave? To come back with vowels polished smooth, carrying a tote bag from a museum gift shop, pretending I’d never wanted acrylic nails with tiny diamonds on them?

I wanted them. God, I wanted them.

I wanted cherry-red lipstick and white stilettos and a dress so tight it made respectability cross the street. I wanted to stand beneath the chemical halo of hairspray while women called each other *babe* and passed around gossip hot as chips. I wanted gold chains, ankle bracelets, frosted shadow; wanted to be excessive, obvious, impossible to mistake for tasteful. But desire was treated like a dog I had to train not to bark.

“Don’t cheapen yourself.”

Cheap. That was the word crouched behind everything. Cheap fabric, cheap scent, cheap girls. As if money had never been the point. As if working-class women hadn’t made theatre from the pound shop, armour from hoops, ceremony from a Saturday night. As if glamour wasn’t something we invented because nobody was going to hand us beauty without an invoice.

So I read Shakespeare. I read him hard. I underlined blood, appetite, women going mad in corridors. I wore the blazer. I won prizes. I let them call me articulate, that little biscuit they give you for making your mouth behave. At interviews I sat with my knees together and spoke of “opportunity” while my mother’s voice banged around inside me, broad and bright and alive.

Sometimes I think the blazer is still on me.

Sometimes I’m forty years old in a bathroom mirror, putting on lipstick, and I hear the old warnings: too red, too much, too obvious. I twist the tube higher.

More.

That’s the word I was taught to fear. Too much makeup, too much skin, too much want. Women like us were allowed dignity only if we dressed it in borrowed clothes. A crisp white shirt. A neutral pump. A tasteful stud.

But I remember Auntie June outside the salon, ash trembling at the end of her cigarette, laughing so hard she had to grab the wall. I remember thinking: there. There is a woman no blazer could translate.

I paint my mouth red enough to start an argument.

Then I say Shakespeare aloud in the accent I was born with.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a compact piece of feminist experimental fiction using colloquial speech, minimal punctuation, fashion-brand references, painful mother-daughter memories, and the closing declaration: “But now, I said now I’m doin cheap.”
counterfactuals.output:
mum taught me womanhood in the Zara fitting room  
chin up gut in don’t ask what it costs  
she zipped me into silence like it was Chanel  

years later I found her crying into a Primark bag  
said grandma called her cheap when she chose college over a wedding  
said freedom always looks trashy to somebody  

I remembered her slapping lipstick off my mouth  
remembered how sorry her hand looked afterward  
two girls in one mirror pretending one of us was the mother  

so I wore the red dress  
boots loud as unpaid women  
labels cut out  
price tags swinging  

she asked what’re you doin honey  

“But now, I said now I’m doin cheap.”
